title: Algiers under the night bombers, May–June 1943
lede: Three nights when Battery C, 62nd Coast Artillery (AA), 4 miles west of Algiers, fired on raiders: 12 May, 13 May and 4 June 1943. The battery's own reports beside the RAF night fighters' record book, the city's newspaper, the Allied communiqués, and the attackers' side: the German Naval Staff's war diary and the Italian and German communiqués.

title: The oiler Kazahaya, 6 October 1943
lede: The fleet oiler Kazahaya, sailing alone for Truk, met two American submarines on 6 October 1943, each on its own patrol. STEELHEAD hit her first, before dawn; TINOSA found her that morning and attacked twice, and she sank in the evening. The boats' war patrol reports beside her own signals, kept in the 2nd Destroyer Squadron's diary, on one GMT clock.

title: Filignano and Selvone, 12 January 1944: the raid at 1500
lede: Two batteries of the 2nd Battalion, 67th Coast Artillery (AA), 2.5 km apart in the hills north of Venafro, fired on the same German raid at 1500 on 12 January 1944, the day the French Expeditionary Corps opened its attack toward Sant'Elia and Atina on the Fifth Army's right. Battery F at Selvone logged "12 ME-109 bombing mission, 2 planes destroyed"; Battery G at Filignano, "12 FW 190's, dive bombing ... Two destroyed". Beside them, the German XIV Panzer Corps' reports of the same day.

title: Shelled on the Winter Line: the 67th CA (AA)'s batteries by Venafro and Acquafondata, February 1944
lede: Two batteries of the 2nd Battalion, 67th Coast Artillery (AA) (from 20 March 1944 the 894th AAA AW Bn), giving antiaircraft protection to the field artillery in the hills between Venafro and Cassino, and what the German XIV Panzer Corps reported about its fire on the same days. Battery E was at Lucenteforte, by Venafro, with half its guns detached near Sant'Elia from 10 to 23 Feb; it had men wounded on 14 and 16 Feb. Battery H moved up near Acquafondata on 12 Feb; its gun positions were shelled at 1500 on 21 Feb.

title: Convoy TAMA-17, 29–30 April 1944
lede: BANG's first attacks: four approaches on convoy TAMA-17 west of Luzon over the night of 29–30 April, with PARCHE and TINOSA closing in on her reports. Every mark is a position or attack typed into the boats' war patrol reports, beside the Japanese record of the same minutes, on one GMT clock.

title: Convoy TE-04, 3–4 May 1944
lede: TINOSA found convoy TE-04 north of Luzon on the morning of 3 May and reported it to PARCHE and BANG; by the early hours of the 4th the three boats had attacked it in turn, and five of its six ships were gone. The boats' war patrol reports beside the escort division's record, on one GMT clock.

title: A lone tanker, 14 June 1944
lede: BANG's first attack of her second patrol, on a tanker alone, as typed on her attack sheet. No Japanese record of it has been found yet.

title: Convoy HI-67, 29 June 1944
lede: BANG's attack on convoy HI-67, bound from Moji for Singapore by way of Manila, as typed on her attack sheets, beside the escort division's chart of the same afternoon.

title: Convoy No. 91, 3–4 July 1944
lede: SEAHORSE's and BANG's attacks on convoy No. 91 southwest of Pratas Island, as typed on their attack sheets, beside the Hong Kong fleet's table of the destroyer Kuri's reports.

title: Convoy MOMA-01, 12 July 1944
lede: THRESHER found a southbound convoy on the night of 11 July and the four boats closed on it. APOGON attacked first, at 0304 on the 12th (Tokyo time), heard three hits and was rammed by a freighter of the convoy, bending her periscope shears; PIRANHA attacked at 0656 and sank a troop transport. GUARDFISH and THRESHER tracked it and were driven off by its escort. The boats' war patrol reports beside the escort division's record, on one GMT clock.

title: Convoy TAMA-21C, 16–17 July 1944
lede: PIRANHA found the convoy at night and reported it to the pack; she attacked it at 0944 on 16 July (Tokyo time) and Seattle Maru, carrying troops, sank. The convoy went on in two parts, one standing by for the rescue. That night GUARDFISH attacked the larger part, ten ships, and THRESHER a group of six about fifty miles to the north; by 0345 on the 17th the Japanese record counted five more ships sunk. The boats' war patrol reports beside the escort division's record, on one GMT clock.

title: Convoy MI-11, 30–31 July 1944
lede: HAMMERHEAD found the convoy before dawn on 30 July, reported it to STEELHEAD and PARCHE at 0420 and attacked it from its port side at 0531 and 0537 (Tokyo time); STEELHEAD tracked it south all day and reported it to PARCHE. From 0332 on the 31st (Tokyo time) the two boats attacked it in turn off the north-west corner of Luzon; PARCHE made eight attacks in thirty-four minutes. The boats' war patrol reports beside the Navy's summary of the night, on one GMT clock.

title: Convoy No. 3905, 9 September 1944
lede: BANG's attacks on convoy No. 3905, bound from Yokosuka for Haha-jima, as typed on her attack sheets, with her depth log and the Yokosuka Guard Squadron's diary of the same afternoon.

title: Convoy TAKA-909, 19 September 1944
lede: BANG's attacks on convoy TAKA-909 east of Formosa, as typed on her attack sheets, with her depth log and the 4th Surface Escort Division's record of the day.

title: A convoy east of Formosa, 20–21 September 1944
lede: BANG's last two attacks of her third patrol, on a convoy she found by its escorts' sound pinging, as typed on her attack sheets. No Japanese record of them has been found yet.

title: Convoy TAKA-206, 22–23 November 1944
lede: The three boats' torpedo attacks of 22–23 November 1944, as typed on their attack sheets, beside the log the convoy's minesweeper W-15 kept of the same night. Times are converted to GMT, so BANG and SHAD (zone K) and the Japanese escorts (zone I) share one clock.

title: The Bulge, the Sauer and Sibret, 16 December 1944 - 3 January 1945
lede: On the morning of 16 December 1944 the German attack in the Ardennes reaches the 9th Armored Division's quiet sector on the Sauer, held by the 60th Armored Infantry Battalion; for five days the battalion and Combat Command A hold the southern shoulder between Beaufort and Ermsdorf. On the 26th the command is sent west, and from the 27th to 3 January it fights beside the corridor just opened to Bastogne, at Sibret and Chenogne. Told here from the battalion's own after action reports for December and January, as a transcription gives them, beside the German side as the Army's official history tells it; no German record is read yet.

title: A small freighter in the Yellow Sea, 10 February 1945
lede: BANG's one torpedo attack of her fifth patrol, as typed on her attack sheet, with her depth log. Times are converted to GMT, with Tokyo time alongside.

title: The Remagen bridge, 7-17 March 1945
lede: The 9th Armored Division's Combat Command B finds the Ludendorff railroad bridge at Remagen standing on the afternoon of 7 March 1945 and crosses it; for ten days the Germans try to bring it down from the air, with artillery, with V-2s and with swimmers, and on the afternoon of 17 March it collapses. Told here from one record so far: Headquarters III Corps' after action report for March 1945 (its narrative, its G-2 report and its engineer journal).

title: USS Haynsworth (DD-700), 6 April 1945
lede: The kamikaze hit on USS Haynsworth, on picket station 12 miles from Task Group 58.3's carriers off Okinawa, on the first day of Japan's mass kamikaze offensive. Her own reports beside the other ships of the group and the Japanese records of the planes sent against them.

title: BANG rescues Ensign Donald E. Corzine, 21–22 April 1945
lede: Hit by flak over Ishigaki airfield on the afternoon of 21 April 1945, a CHENANGO Hellcat pilot spent fourteen hours in his raft before BANG, sent from her lifeguard station off Formosa, took him aboard. BANG's report, his squadron's action report and the Miyako garrison's telegram of the same day, on one GMT clock.

title: Neuburg an der Donau, 26 April 1945
lede: Six Me 262 jets of JV 44, led by Adolf Galland on his last mission, attack a formation of the 17th Bomb Group's B-26s over the Danube at Neuburg, as the 45th Infantry Division crosses the river below. Three records that never mention each other describe the same five minutes: the 106th AAA AW Battalion's history (its batteries fired on the jets), the 189th Field Artillery Battalion's history (it watched from Bergen, just north-west of the town), and the three Missing Air Crew Reports. The German side is Galland's own account, written in 1953; JV 44's records are still to find.
